title: Compilers and Executables
description: What happens between pressing Run and seeing output: compiling to machine code, then running it.

content.value: When you press Run, your code does not go straight to the computer. First it is **compiled**: a program called a **compiler** checks it and translates it. Then the translation runs.

steps.label: main.cpp
steps.detail: your code, text you can read

steps.label: Output
steps.detail: what you see in the terminal

content.title: What happens when you press Run
content.caption: On this platform the compiler is `g++`. If it finds a mistake, it stops and tells you, and the run step never happens.
Even this one line goes through both steps.

content.question: You forget a semicolon and press Run. What happens?
options: `g++` stops with an error, and nothing runs
The program runs and skips that line
The compiler adds the semicolon for you
It runs, then crashes at the end
content.explain: Compiling is a checking step. A mistake there means step two, running, never happens.

items.sub: The processor's own language: raw numbers it understands directly.
The file of machine code `g++` makes. On Windows it ends in `.exe`; on Mac and Linux it usually has no ending.
Your `.cpp` file. You write and edit this one, never the executable.

content.real: A book translated into one reader's language
content.concept: An executable built for one kind of machine
content.text: Nothing needs translating while it runs, which is why C++ is so fast. But a Windows executable won't run on a Mac or a phone. To run there, compile the same source code again on that machine.

content.question: Which file do **you** write and edit?
content.explain: You write the `.cpp` file (source code). The compiler makes the executable for you.

content.value: Building an executable really happens in three stages. Knowing them helps you understand error messages.

steps.label: Preprocessor
steps.detail: handles `#` lines: `#include <iostream>` pastes in the printing tools

steps.label: Compiler
steps.detail: checks your code and turns it into machine code

steps.label: Linker
steps.detail: joins it to the library code that makes `cout` work

content.title: From main.cpp to main.exe
content.caption: If any stage fails, you get an error and no executable.
Without the `#include` line, the compiler would never have heard of `cout`.

content.question: Which stage handles the line `#include <iostream>`?
content.explain: Every line starting with `#` is handled by the preprocessor, before the compiler proper sees your code.

items: There is more than one compiler: `g++` (part of a toolset called **GCC**), `clang`, and Microsoft's Visual Studio. They all read the same language.
C++ comes in versions named after the year they were agreed: C++11, C++14, C++17, C++20. Each adds features.
This platform compiles your code as **C++17**: modern and supported everywhere.

parts.label: compiler
parts.note: The program that builds your code.

parts.label: version
parts.note: Which version of C++ to use.

content.title: Step 1 by hand: compile in a terminal
content.caption: Step 2 is typing `./main` to run the executable.
The Run button types both commands for you.

practice.question: Write a program that prints the two steps in order: one line saying Step 1: compile, and one saying Step 2: run.

quiz.question: What does `g++` do?
options: Runs your program and shows the output.
Checks your code and translates it into an executable.
quiz.explain: `g++` is the compiler. It reads your `.cpp` file, reports any mistakes, and writes an executable full of machine code.

quiz.question: What is inside an executable?
options: Machine code: instructions the processor understands directly.
quiz.explain: The compiler translates your C++ into the processor's own language. That is why the executable can run without anything translating it on the fly.

quiz.question: You built your program on a Windows laptop. How do you run it on a Mac?
options: Copy the .exe file across; it runs anywhere.
You cannot: C++ only works on Windows.
Compile the same source code again for the Mac.
quiz.explain: Machine code is specific to one kind of machine. The source code is the portable part, so you rebuild it for each system.

quiz.question: Which stage handles `#include <iostream>`?
options: The program itself, while it runs.
quiz.explain: Lines starting with `#` are handled first, by the preprocessor. `#include` pastes in the declarations the compiler needs to know about `cout`.
